label: text
text: LEGED FORGERS GANG

label: text
text: Believed by the Police to be a member of a well-organised gang of forgers who, working in conjunction with confederates in the Post Office, obtain information from letters, forge chops and demand notes. Au Cheong, 33, was charged on remand before Mr. K. E. Lindsell at the Central Maristleacy this morning with attempting to obtain $1,000 by false retentions with intent to defraud.

label: text
text:
ant. Yeung Kwai-yad and Mr. D. McCallum defended the accused.
At the previous hearing the complainant gave evidence regarding the receipt of letters which aroused his suspicion and led to his taking the matter to the Police. The case was put in the hands of Det. Sub-Inspector Lane who arranged for a Chinese de-tive to go to the complainant's office, No. 21, New Street, dis-pursed as a clerk. Accused called by appointment and was handed two $500 notes which had previously been marked. "Leaving the office, he was followed and subsequently arrested."

label: text
text:
At the commencement of this morning's hearing Mr. Prior informed the Magistrate that he had been unable to secure certified copies of his translations of the Chinese letters. "The Supreme Court refuse to translate them," said counsel, "and the Secretary for Chinese Affairs says he is too busy." He, Mr. Prior, was therefore quite helpless in the matter and would ask His Worship to allow him to get the various witnesses to state what they understood by them. Mr. McCallum raising no objection to the suggested procedure. His Worship allowed the application.
Lam Kwok-an, accountant in the employ of the firm from whom the letter was supposed to have been sent, said that he had not written it; it was undoubtedly a forgery as he was in a position to know about every letter that left his office. The letter was not in the handwriting of anyone in his office. His firm, as a matter of fact, knew nothing whatever of the $1,000 demanded.
Case proceeding.

label: text
text: HEAD OVER HEELS.

label: text
text:
The son of Mr. Tong Yat-cheun, J.P., appeared this morning before Mr. J. H. B. Nihill at the Kowloon Magistracy charged with assaulting a bus conductor, and refusing to alight from a bus when ordered.
The complainant conductor, alleged that defendant boarded his bus while it was in motion at Yaumati, despite his refusal to admit him because there was no room. Complainant also alleged that he was kicked by defendant who on jumping from the "bus" fell "head over heels."
His Worship imposed a fine of $10 on the first charge and dismissed the second.

label: text
text: Before the political trouble in June, sales of opium had decreased to 6,000 tails per week; and for the remainder of the year to about 4,000 taels per week. The great decrease is partly due to the political troubles, partly to the large amounts of cheap Chinese opium, and partly due to the large amounts of Macao opium smuggled into the Colony.

text: Marching With An Anti-Red

label: text
text:
General Yang Sen has moved a great many troops downstream during the past day or two. He has captured several small river ports above Hankow and in general consolidated his position within striking distance of Hankow. Yesterday we reported that his troops had looted the city of Patang, a rather unimportant port a few miles up river beyond Ichang. This report came from a reliable source, though details as to the looting have not yet been received.
On the other hand General Yang Sen is reported to be advancing upon Hankow with a definite anti-Red purpose and this may possibly account for the reported evacuation of Hanyang by the Southern.

label: paragraph_title

label: paragraph_title
text: CONTINUOUS PRAYER IN CATHEDRAL.

label: paragraph_title
text: HELPERS WANTED:

label: text
text: On St. Andrewstide, the November number of "St. John's"

label: text
text: "The eve of St. Andrew's day has been for many years the day appointed as a day of special prayer for the extension of the Kingdom of God amongst non-Christian people." It has long been observed as a day of continuous prayer in the Cathedral, different people taking a quarter of an hour and spending the time in the Cathedral in prayer. The Chaplain will be very glad to hear from any who like to take part in the work. It is, noticeable how the missionary work of the Church has spread and increased since the initiation of the Day of Intercession in the year 1872. At the present time the four reports issued by the Missionary Council of the National Assembly of the Church of England have shown how pressing is the need of a great increase in the number of workers and in the amount contributed by our Church to the evangelisation of the world. Empire involves responsibility, and we of the British Empire are bound to see that we do our part in spreading the Christian message which has been the foundation of our own national life."
